title: Desired state: Deployments, ReplicaSets and Pods
summary: A Deployment declares what you want; controllers keep making it true. Learn which object acts after a change to replicas or to the Pod template.
prereqText: You need to know what a container image and a running container are (from Docker). Nothing about Kubernetes is assumed.

blocks.html: With docker compose you might run docker compose up -d --scale web=3. If a container dies, nothing brings it back unless you add a restart policy, and changing the image means you stop and start things yourself. Now imagine you edit one file saying "I want 3 copies of web" and a process keeps checking that this is true, forever, replacing what dies and replacing versions gradually. That file, for Kubernetes, is a Deployment. Your goal today: look at a change you could make to it and predict what the system does.

blocks.prompt: A Deployment web currently has 3 Pods. You apply it twice: first with replicas: 5, later with image: example/web:v2 in the Pod template. Which statement is best?
options: Both changes create a new ReplicaSet and replace every Pod
Only the image change creates a new ReplicaSet; the replicas change scales the existing one
Only the replicas change creates a new ReplicaSet, because the number of Pods changes

feedback.0: Misconception: every edit replaces Pods. The docs say a rollout is triggered only by a Pod template change; scaling does not trigger one.
feedback.2: Misconception: more Pods means a new ReplicaSet. A ReplicaSet already has a replica count, so the controller just changes it.

blocks.explanation: A Deployment rollout is triggered if and only if its Pod template (.spec.template) changes; other updates such as scaling do not trigger a rollout. [source]

blocks.html: Think of a thermostat. You set the target temperature (the desired state); the thermostat measures the room (the current state) and switches heating on or off to close the gap, over and over. Kubernetes controllers are this kind of loop. [source] A Deployment is your target, and the controllers are the thermostat.
blocks.limits: A thermostat adjusts one number. A Deployment controller manages other objects (ReplicaSets), which have their own controller managing Pods. Also, the cluster may never be perfectly stable; the docs say that is fine while controllers keep running. The loop is also not instantaneous: you saw nothing happen "at the moment you apply", only a recorded desired state that controllers then act on.

blocks.purpose: Show who owns whom: Deployment to ReplicaSets to Pods, and which field each controller reads.
blocks.alt: A three-level ownership diagram. A Deployment named web with replicas 3 and a Pod template version v1 owns a ReplicaSet web-hash1 with 3 Pods. After the template changes to v2, the Deployment also owns a second ReplicaSet web-hash2 which gets Pods while the first ReplicaSet is scaled down. Pods carry a pod-template-hash label that matches their ReplicaSet.

blocks.title: What each object does
blocks.html:
A Pod runs your container. You rarely create Pods directly. A ReplicaSet has three things: a selector (which Pods it owns), a replica count, and a Pod template used to create missing Pods. It creates or deletes Pods until the count matches, and records itself in each Pod's metadata.ownerReferences. [source]

A Deployment sits one level up. You describe a desired state in it and the Deployment controller changes the actual state to the desired state at a controlled rate. [source] It does this by managing ReplicaSets. The docs recommend using a Deployment rather than a bare ReplicaSet unless you need custom update orchestration or no updates at all, and they caution against managing ReplicaSets that a Deployment owns. [source]

Two kinds of change, two behaviours.

  • Change replicas: the existing (current) ReplicaSet's count changes. No new ReplicaSet, no rollout. [source]
  • Change anything in .spec.template (image, labels, probes, env): the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet for the new template and, with the default RollingUpdate strategy, scales it up while scaling the old one down. This is a rollout.

To tell ReplicaSets apart, the Deployment adds a pod-template-hash label to each ReplicaSet and its Pods (and the name of the ReplicaSet ends in that hash). Do not edit it. [source] Defaults you will use later: strategy.type is RollingUpdate (the alternative Recreate kills all old Pods before creating new ones), and the Deployment keeps old ReplicaSets (10 by default) so you can roll back. [source]

Simplification: .spec.replicas is optional and defaults to 1; if a horizontal autoscaler manages the count, you normally do not set it in the manifest. That interaction is outside this course.

blocks.title: Reading a manifest and predicting the controller

steps.html:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: example/web:v1

Desired state: 3 Pods built from the template. Course example, not from the docs. Note selector must match the template labels, and in apps/v1 it is immutable after creation. [source]

steps.prompt: You apply this. What objects exist after the controllers settle?
steps.html: One Deployment, one ReplicaSet (named web-<hash>) with 3 Pods, all labelled app=web plus the pod-template-hash.

steps.prompt: Now you change only replicas: 3 to replicas: 6 and apply. What happens?
steps.html: The Deployment controller sees desired 6 versus current 3, and the same ReplicaSet's count becomes 6 (ReplicaSet controller creates 3 more Pods). The template is unchanged, so no new ReplicaSet and no rollout.
The template changed, so a new ReplicaSet (new hash) is created and gradually scaled up to 6 while the old one is scaled down to 0. The old ReplicaSet is kept, with 0 Pods, for rollback.

blocks.result: Rule of thumb: replicas changes the count of the current ReplicaSet; a template change creates a new ReplicaSet. Prediction is the skill: name the object that changes first.

blocks.instructions: This is a simulation written for this course, not a cluster. Step through three events. Before each step is revealed, answer the prediction. Click a component to read what it does.
blocks.debrief: You should have noticed that the replicas change touched only the ReplicaSet count, while the template change created a new object. The same Deployment, two different controller responses. The scaling step involves no hash change; the rollout step does.

config.title: Which controller acts after each edit? (simulation)

nodes.label: Deployment web
nodes.html: Holds replicas and the Pod template. Its controller creates and scales ReplicaSets.

nodes.label: ReplicaSet v1
nodes.html: Selector + count + template for the v1 Pods.

steps.html: State: Deployment web (3, v1) → ReplicaSet v1 (3) → 3 Pods v1.

predict.prompt: Which objects are involved in reaching 5 Pods?
options: Deployment and ReplicaSet v1 only; ReplicaSet v1 count becomes 5
A new ReplicaSet v2 is created with 5 Pods
All 3 existing Pods are deleted and 5 are created
predict.explanation: Scaling does not change the template, so the existing ReplicaSet is scaled to 5 and creates 2 more Pods.

steps.html: State: Deployment (5, v1) → ReplicaSet v1 (5) → 5 Pods v1. Existing Pods are untouched.

steps.event: You change the image: v1 → v2

predict.prompt: What does the Deployment controller create?
options: A new ReplicaSet v2, scaled up as v1 is scaled down
Nothing; Pods are updated in place
Only new Pods, owned directly by the Deployment
predict.explanation: A new Pod template means a new ReplicaSet. Pods are never mutated in place; they are replaced.

steps.html: State (during rollout, one possible moment): ReplicaSet v1 (4) and ReplicaSet v2 (2) shortly after the change. The exact numbers depend on the rolling-update limits, which is the next lesson.
State: ReplicaSet v2 (5), ReplicaSet v1 (0, kept for rollback), 5 Pods v2.

assumptions: Illustrative simulation of the documented behaviour, not output from a real cluster.
The in-between Pod counts are one possible moment, not an exact trace; limits are explained in the next lesson.
Scheduling, image pulls and autoscaling are omitted.

blocks.task: Take the manifest in the worked example. For each edit, write (a) whether a new ReplicaSet is created, and (b) the objects whose fields change. Edits: 1) replicas: 3 to 2; 2) add a label tier: frontend to .spec.template.metadata.labels (and keep the selector valid); 3) change the Deployment's metadata.name labels only (not the template).
hints: Labels of the Deployment object itself are not part of the Pod template.
rubric: Edit 1: no new ReplicaSet; ReplicaSet count goes to 2
Edit 2: new ReplicaSet (template changed, labels are part of it)
blocks.solution: 1) Same ReplicaSet scaled to 2 (it deletes a Pod). 2) New ReplicaSet and a rollout, because labels in the template are part of it; the docs give "labels or container images of the template" as example triggers. [source] 3) No rollout: the Pod template is unchanged. Check: this is derived from the "if and only if .spec.template changes" rule.

blocks.task: A colleague says: "I bumped replicas to 10 and nothing was replaced, but I also changed the image in the same commit and now all my Pods are being replaced. Is Kubernetes inconsistent?" Write 3-4 sentences explaining what actually happened, using the words ReplicaSet and Pod template.
rubric: Names the Pod template change as the trigger
States replicas alone does not trigger a rollout
blocks.model: Both edits were applied. The replicas change alone would only have scaled the current ReplicaSet. The image change is inside the Pod template, which creates a new ReplicaSet and a rollout that replaces Pods gradually. So the result is consistent: the template change dominates what you see, and the new ReplicaSet is scaled to 10.

blocks.html: Check your understanding. Your first attempt is recorded as performance; later attempts are practice.

questions.prompt: Which edit triggers a rollout (a new ReplicaSet)?
options: image: web:v1 to web:v2 in the Pod template
questions.explanation: Only changes to .spec.template trigger a rollout. Scaling by editing the manifest or by kubectl scale does not.

feedback.0: That scales the current ReplicaSet only.
feedback.2: Scaling, by any route, does not change the template.

questions.prompt: Which object keeps the Pods running at the right count and records ownership in metadata.ownerReferences?
questions.explanation: A ReplicaSet links to its Pods through their ownerReferences and creates or deletes Pods to match its count. The Deployment manages ReplicaSets.

feedback.0: The Deployment creates and scales ReplicaSets; Pods belong to a ReplicaSet.
feedback.2: The kubelet runs containers on a node; it does not own replica counts.

questions.prompt: After a rollout from v1 to v2 completes, what is the old ReplicaSet's state by default?
options: Kept with 0 Pods (up to 10 old ones are retained by default)
questions.explanation: Old ReplicaSets are kept (default 10) so you can roll back. Their Pod count is 0.

feedback.0: If it were deleted, you would lose the ability to roll back to that revision.
feedback.2: At the end of a completed rollout no old Pods remain.

questions.prompt: In your own words: what does it mean that a Deployment declares "desired state"? Include what the controller does about it.
rubric: Says you declare what you want (spec) rather than commands
Says a controller compares current with desired and acts
questions.model: The spec says what should be true (for example 3 Pods of this template). A controller keeps comparing the actual state with it and creates, scales or deletes objects to close the gap, continuously.

blocks.task: New situation. A team runs api with replicas: 4. In one pull request they (a) add an environment variable LOG_LEVEL=debug to the container and (b) change replicas to 2 to save cost. Predict, in order, what the Deployment controller does, and say what you would see in kubectl get rs afterwards (counts per ReplicaSet). Do not run anything; reason from the rules.
rubric: Identifies the env var as a Pod template change that creates a new ReplicaSet
Identifies replicas as the desired count for the new template
Predicts old ReplicaSet at 0 and new at 2 after the rollout
Notes the old ReplicaSet is kept for rollback
blocks.model: The env var is inside the Pod template, so a new ReplicaSet is created and a rollout begins. The new desired count is 2, so the end state is new ReplicaSet at 2, old ReplicaSet at 0 (retained for rollback). The replicas change alone would not have caused a rollout, but the env var does. Mid-rollout counts depend on the update limits (next lesson).

blocks.prompt: Explain in your own words, as you would to a colleague who knows Docker: what is a ReplicaSet for, and why does a Deployment create a new one when the Pod template changes? Then compare with the model in the lesson.
